scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

This is a shared geographic narrative, not a claim of continuous state identity. The map’s gaps do not represent depopulation. No unverified successor targets are added. The opening 1220 boundary is an archaeological reference point; occupation began earlier, and neither the 1511 phase boundary nor a site’s abandonment marks Indigenous extinction.

The Los Buchillones chronology and pilings interpretation come from the 2006 paper’s accessible abstract; access to its full text is not claimed. The 2013 Spanish-language collection study was downloaded and read, especially printed pages 10 to 17. It combines excavated artifacts and older collections. Suggested cutting functions and ceremonial uses are interpretations, not observations of named individuals. No exact household sizes, ownership or single date for every object is inferred.

The 2001 Gabinete de Arqueología issue was downloaded and its relevant reports read. Habana 958 is distinguished from other Havana houses and from later fill within its own latrine. The source prints implausible centimetre units for metre-scale dimensions; no dimensions are adopted. No particular bone is assigned to a menu without species analysis. The two game counters from El Padre do not establish the rules of a game, a specific player or an uncoerced plantation life.

El Lector is represented by the publisher’s description and contents, not an assertion of having read the whole book. The text does not repeat unsupported cigar-brand naming stories, factory literacy rates, claims that all workers were illiterate, or the publisher’s general comparison of workers’ cultural sophistication. No photograph of Tampa is relabelled Havana.

PAHO’s historical account distinguishes Finlay’s 1881 hypothesis from the 1900 Yellow Fever Board experiments. Its sweeping claim of eradication throughout the Caribbean is not adopted. No modern clinical guidance or medical efficacy is inferred from historical plant knowledge.

UNESCO recognition dates identify published accounts of living practices, not invention years. The card avoids claiming that all Cubans practise one tradition. Cassava bread is a multinational tradition with local variation; a short heritage description is not a safe preparation recipe. Punto is described as ten-line verse without reproducing the English page’s imprecise octameter terminology.

The Smithsonian’s 2015 workshop image is a specific family-learning example in eastern Cuba. It supports living Indigenous presence and knowledge-sharing, not clinical results or an unchanging culture. Child names are omitted. The exhibition announcement’s caption and main text were read through the indexed page after direct opening timed out.

The colonial overview and the 2006 Library of Congress profile are used selectively for institutional chronology. The profile’s claim that Cuban history began in 1492 and that Indigenous peoples were eliminated is rejected in light of archaeological and Smithsonian evidence. Its sweeping claims about prosperity, racial relations and post-revolutionary politics are not adopted. Its inaccurate almost-five-year occupation duration is not repeated.

The brief British occupation concerns Havana, not sovereignty over all Cuba. The UNESCO Courier article’s anachronistic reference to dynamite in 1762 and its royal telescope anecdote are excluded. Only the capture, duration and recovery of the city are used.

The Office of the Historian distinguishes its May 19 installation wording from the May 20 transfer of occupation authority. The card uses the latter, consistent with the Library of Congress independence date. The Platt Amendment’s intervention provisions are distinguished from the ongoing Guantánamo base arrangement. The post-1959 period is a broad historical window, not a claim that Fidel Castro governs today.

Several UNESCO, PAHO, Smithsonian and Library of Congress HTML pages failed on direct opening; the relevant full indexed descriptions were read. Archaeological PDFs and the country profile were read locally after download. This access limitation is recorded without claiming a full book or paywalled article was inspected.
The new narrative is author-checked against the cited passages and awaits independent historical review.

identityEvidence.assessment: The two records cover the island of Cuba, with near-identical extents. Their 1530 to 1715 and 1914 to present intervals are imported map windows, not the start or end of Spanish colonisation, independence or the republic. Geometry is unchanged and not certified.

sharedAssociations.basis: Both imported outlines depict Cuba. This island-wide historical narrative distinguishes Spanish colonial rule, the U.S. occupation and later Cuban governments rather than treating them as one state. See identityEvidence.
